Nationwide General Strike Disrupts Peruvian Economy, Energy Sector Impacted

LIMA – Economic activity across Peru ground to a halt on Monday as thousands of workers from a broad range of sectors joined a general strike called by major union federations, with energy producers such as Enel Generacion Peru SAA among those affected. The strike, which began early in the morning, has caused widespread disruption in transportation, public services, and key industries, and shows no signs of abating as negotiations remain at an impasse.

The Confederación General de Trabajadores del Perú (CGTP), the country’s largest trade union, organized the strike in response to stalled wage negotiations, rising living costs, and concerns over labor conditions. The action has seen participation from public transport workers, healthcare staff, teachers, and employees in the mining and energy sectors, amplifying its nationwide impact.

In Lima, major avenues saw reduced bus and taxi services, with long lines forming at the few terminals still operating. “We’re asking for fair wages and better working conditions. The cost of living keeps going up, but our pay doesn’t,” said José Medina, a union delegate at a protest outside the Ministry of Labor.

The energy sector has not been spared. Enel Generacion Peru SAA, one of the country’s largest electricity producers, confirmed that a number of its facilities are operating with reduced personnel due to worker participation in the strike. Company spokesperson Ana Valverde stated, “We are prioritizing the safety of our staff and continuity of essential services, but some non-critical operations have been temporarily scaled back. We are closely monitoring the situation and hope for a swift resolution.”

The Peruvian Association of Exporters warned that the strike could have a significant impact on shipments of agricultural and mining products if disruptions persist. "Every day of work lost puts pressure on production schedules and international commitments," said analyst Rafael Gamarra.

Hospitals in several regions reported delays in non-emergency care, while schools in Lima, Arequipa, and Trujillo cancelled classes as teachers joined the strike. In the city of Chiclayo, municipal offices closed, with only emergency services available.

The Ministry of Labor issued a statement urging both sides to return to the negotiating table. “Dialogue is the only way forward to restore normal activity and address the legitimate concerns of workers,” said Minister Rosa Navarro.

Despite the government’s call for calm, union leaders indicated that the strike would continue until concrete proposals are presented. As of Monday evening, no breakthrough had been reported, and the economic effects of the strike were expected to intensify if the action enters a second day.
